lesson.title: Foam Cups and Real Chemistry: The Coffee Cup Calorimeter
lesson.summary: A coffee cup calorimeter is a simple, low cost device, essentially a nested pair of foam cups, that measures heat flow for reactions in aqueous solution at constant atmospheric pressure, giving the enthalpy change directly.
lesson.body:
One of the most useful calorimeters in a general chemistry lab is also one of the cheapest: two nested styrofoam coffee cups, a lid with a hole for a thermometer, and a stirrer. Despite its simplicity, this setup is precise enough to measure the heat of reactions carried out in aqueous solution, such as acid base neutralizations or salts dissolving in water. The reaction happens directly in the water inside the cup, and that same water serves as the substance whose temperature change you track and plug into q = m c delta T.

In the language of the systems you have already studied, a coffee cup calorimeter approximates a closed system. Matter, the dissolved reactants and the water, stays inside the cup, but the styrofoam walls are not perfect insulators, so some energy can still leak out to the surrounding room as heat. This is different from an isolated system, where neither matter nor energy crosses the boundary, which is the idealization a bomb calorimeter aims for instead.

The single most important feature of the coffee cup calorimeter is that it is open to the atmosphere, so the reaction happens at a constant pressure equal to atmospheric pressure. As you will learn in the enthalpy chapter, heat measured at constant pressure is exactly equal to the enthalpy change of the process, q(constant pressure) = delta H. That means a coffee cup calorimeter hands you enthalpy change directly, with no extra correction needed, which is exactly why it is the standard tool for measuring the enthalpy of neutralization, dissolution, and dilution reactions.

Two simplifying assumptions make the arithmetic manageable. First, the specific heat capacity of the dilute solution is assumed to equal that of pure water, since the dissolved solutes are a small fraction of the total mass. Second, the heat capacity of the foam cup and thermometer themselves is treated as negligible, since foam absorbs almost no heat compared to water. As an example, a student combines 50.0 mL of 1.0 M HCl with 50.0 mL of 1.0 M NaOH inside a coffee cup calorimeter. Both solutions start at 21.0 degrees C, and after the neutralization reaction the mixture settles at 27.5 degrees C. Assuming the combined solution has a mass of 100.0 g (density approximately 1.00 g/mL) and a specific heat capacity of 4.18 J/(g times degree C), the heat released is q = m c delta T = (100.0 g)(4.18 J/(g times degree C))(27.5 minus 21.0) = (418 J/degree C)(6.5 degrees C) = 2,717 J, or 2.72 kJ, absorbed by the solution. Since the reaction released this heat, q(reaction) = negative 2.72 kJ, and because this measurement was made at constant pressure, delta H(reaction) = negative 2.72 kJ for this particular mixture. To express it per mole, note that 50.0 mL of 1.0 M HCl contains (0.0500 L)(1.0 mol/L) = 0.0500 mol of acid, all of which reacts. Dividing gives delta H = negative 2.72 kJ divided by 0.0500 mol = negative 54.3 kJ/mol, a reasonable, physically sensible value for an acid base neutralization measured this way.
